title: Data Science Environment and Tools
summary: Data scientists live in interactive environments that mix code, output, and notes. Jupyter notebooks let you run code in cells, see results immediately, and document your thinking with Markdown - ideal for exploration and sharing analyses. Managing p
content:
# Data Science Environment and Tools ##### "It worked on my laptop last month" A student in Indore submitted a data science assignment. The evaluator opened the notebook and it failed on cell 3. The student's screenshot showed it running perfectly. The difference: she had `pandas 2.2` installed globally, the evaluator had `1.5`. A method she used did not exist in the older version. She had no `requirements.txt`, so there was no way to know. Then it got worse. She reran her own notebook top to bottom to prove it worked — and it failed too. She had defined a variable in cell 12, deleted the cell, and kept using it. The notebook's *state* held the variable; the notebook's *code* no longer created it. It had been broken for two weeks and she could not tell, because she never restarted the kernel. Both problems have the same root: **an environment you cannot reproduce is an environment you cannot trust.** Today is about setting up so that "it works on my machine" becomes "it works on any machine, including mine tomorrow." ##### Package management: pip, conda, and the modern option Python's ecosystem is its strength and its mess. Three tools you will encounter: **pip** is the standard installer, bundled with Python. It installs from PyPI and works for almost everything. **conda** (via Anaconda or Miniconda) manages packages *and* non-Python dependencies — C libraries, CUDA toolkits, R. It is genuinely useful in scientific computing where a package needs compiled libraries, and it can be slow and heavy. **uv** is the newer Rust-based tool that is dramatically faster and handles environments and lockfiles together. It is increasingly the default in new projects. | | pip + venv | conda / Miniconda | uv | |---|---|---|---| | Speed | Moderate | Slow | Very fast | | Non-Python deps | No | Yes | No | | Lockfile | Manual | `environment.yml` | Automatic `uv.lock` | | Disk footprint | Small | Large (Anaconda ~3 GB) | Small | | Best for | Most projects | GPU/scientific stacks | New projects | The practical recommendation for a beginner: **Miniconda, not full Anaconda.** Anaconda installs 250+ packages you will never use and takes several gigabytes; Miniconda gives you the same tool with nothing preinstalled. Or skip conda entirely and use `venv` plus pip, which is built into Python and sufficient for tabular data science. ##### Virtual environments: why they are not optional A virtual environment is an isolated folder containing its own Python and its own packages. Without one, every project shares the same global installation — so upgrading Pandas for project B silently breaks project A. ```bash # Built-in venv (works everywhere, no extra install) python -m venv .venv # Activate it source .venv/bin/activate # macOS / Linux .venv\Scripts\activate # Windows PowerShell # Now pip installs go INTO this folder only pip install numpy pandas matplotlib jupyterlab pip freeze > requirements.txt # record exact versions deactivate # leave the environment ``` ```bash # Conda equivalent conda create -n dsprep python=3.12 -y conda activate dsprep conda install numpy pandas matplotlib jupyterlab -y conda env export --from-history > environment.yml ``` ```bash # uv — fastest, handles everything uv init my-analysis && cd my-analysis uv add numpy pandas matplotlib jupyterlab uv run jupyter lab # runs inside the env automatically ``` The prompt changes to show the active environment — `(.venv) $` or `(dsprep) $`. If you do not see it, you are not in the environment, and your `pip install` just went global. **Always create the environment inside the project folder and name it `.venv`**, so it is obvious which project it belongs to. Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore` — never commit an environment, commit the *recipe* for it. `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures exact versions. That file is what would have saved the Indore student. Better still, distinguish direct dependencies from transitive ones: ``` # requirements.txt — what I actually asked for pandas==2.2.3 numpy==2.1.2 matplotlib==3.9.2 jupyterlab==4.2.5 ``` ##### Jupyter: how it actually works Jupyter runs a **kernel** — a live Python process — and sends it code from cells. Output comes back and is displayed inline. That architecture explains both its power and its main hazard. The power: you load a 500 MB dataset once, then experiment with it for two hours without reloading. Compare that to a script, which re-reads the file every run. The hazard: **the kernel remembers everything, including code you have deleted.** Cell execution order is whatever you clicked, not top-to-bottom. The `[3]`, `[17]`, `[4]` numbers beside cells are the execution counter, and if they are not ascending, your notebook does not do what it appears to do. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[You write code in a cell] --> B[Shift+Enter sends it to the kernel] B --> C[Kernel executes and keeps all variables in memory] C --> D[Output returns and displays inline] D --> E{Cells run out of order?} E -->|Yes| F[Notebook state != notebook code
Silent, invisible breakage] E -->|No| G[Reproducible] F --> H[Kernel > Restart & Run All to find out] ``` **The single most valuable habit: before you share, commit or submit anything, run Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells.** If it fails, your notebook was already broken and you just found out cheaply. Essential keyboard shortcuts (press `Esc` first for command mode): | Key | Action | |---|---| | `Shift+Enter` | Run cell, move to next | | `Ctrl+Enter` | Run cell, stay | | `Esc` then `A` / `B` | Insert cell above / below | | `Esc` then `M` / `Y` | Convert to Markdown / code | | `Esc` then `D D` | Delete cell | | `Esc` then `Z` | Undo cell deletion | | `Shift+Tab` in a function call | Show the documentation | Useful magic commands: ```python %matplotlib inline # show plots in the notebook %timeit sum(range(1000)) # time a single line %%time # time the whole cell (must be first line) %who # list defined variables %load_ext autoreload # reload imported modules when they change %autoreload 2 !pip list # run a shell command with ! ``` `autoreload` is genuinely useful once you start putting functions in `.py` files — edit the file, and the notebook picks up the change without restarting. ##### Notebook best practices Notebooks are excellent for exploration and terrible as production code. The discipline is knowing which mode you are in. **Structure a notebook like a document, not a scratchpad:** ```markdown # Delivery Performance Analysis — Q2 2026 ## 1. Objective Identify which hubs fell below the 85% on-time threshold and why. ## 2. Setup [imports, configuration, constants — all in ONE cell at the top] ## 3. Load data ## 4. Data quality checks ## 5. Exploration ## 6. Findings ## 7. Next steps ``` Rules that make notebooks survivable: - **All imports in the first code cell.** An import buried in cell 30 means the notebook cannot be read linearly. - **Constants near the top**, not magic numbers scattered through the analysis. - **One idea per cell.** A 60-line cell cannot be re-run selectively, which defeats the point of notebooks. - **Markdown between code cells** explaining *why*, not what. The code shows what. - **Refactor repeated code into functions**, and once a function stabilises, move it to a `.py` file and import it. - **Never leave a cell whose output you cannot reproduce.** - **Clear outputs before committing to Git** — outputs make diffs unreadable and can bloat a repo with embedded images. ```bash pip install nbstripout nbstripout --install # strips outputs automatically on git commit ``` Notebooks are also where secrets leak. Never write an API key in a cell — it goes into the notebook file, which goes into Git, which is public. Use environment variables: ```python import os from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() # reads a .env file (which is gitignored) api_key = os.environ["MY_API_KEY"] ``` ##### Google Colab Colab is a hosted Jupyter environment: no installation, free GPU access, and everything runs in Google's cloud. **Use it when:** your laptop is underpowered, you need a GPU for a few hours, you want to share a runnable notebook with someone instantly, or you are on a machine where you cannot install software. **Be aware that:** sessions disconnect after inactivity and are wiped after roughly 12 hours, the filesystem is temporary, and package versions reset every session. ```python # Persist work by mounting Drive from google.colab import drive drive.mount('/content/drive') # Install anything missing (resets each session) !pip install -q evidently # Upload a file from your machine from google.colab import files uploaded = files.upload() ``` Pin your versions in Colab too — `!pip install pandas==2.2.3` — or your notebook will behave differently next month when Colab's base image updates. ##### Markdown for documentation Markdown is how you write everything around the code: notebook narration, READMEs, documentation. ```markdown # Heading 1 ## Heading 2 **bold**, *italic*, `inline code` - bullet - list - nested 1. numbered 2. list | Hub | On-time % | Status | |-----|-----------|--------| | Panvel | 87.4 | OK | | Kalyan | 68.9 | Review | > A blockquote, useful for highlighting a finding. [Link text](https://example.in) ```python # a fenced code block with syntax highlighting print("hello") ``` $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i$ ← LaTeX works in Jupyter ``` The LaTeX support matters more than you would expect — being able to write the formula next to the code that implements it is one of the genuine advantages of notebooks for learning statistics. ##### A reproducible project layout ``` delivery-analysis/ ├── .venv/ # gitignored ├── .gitignore ├── .env # secrets, gitignored ├── README.md # what this is, how to run it ├── requirements.txt # pinned versions ├── data/ │ ├── raw/ # never edited, often gitignored (large) │ └── processed/ # generated, reproducible ├── notebooks/ │ ├── 01-data-quality.ipynb │ └── 02-exploration.ipynb ├── src/ │ └── helpers.py # functions promoted out of notebooks └── outputs/ └── figures/ ``` Numbered notebooks make the intended order obvious. The `data/raw` versus `data/processed` split enforces a rule worth taking seriously: **raw data is immutable.** Never overwrite the file you downloaded — every transformation writes somewhere new, so you can always start again. A `.gitignore` worth starting from: ``` .venv/ .env __pycache__/ .ipynb_checkpoints/ data/raw/*.csv outputs/ ``` ##### Common mistakes - Installing everything globally and breaking one project by fixing another. - Forgetting to activate the environment, so packages go to the wrong place. - No `requirements.txt`, so nobody — including you — can reproduce the run. - Never restarting the kernel, and shipping a notebook that cannot execute. - Running cells out of order and trusting the output. - Imports scattered through the notebook instead of one cell at the top. - Committing notebooks with outputs, making diffs unreadable. - API keys written directly in a cell and pushed to a public repo. - Editing raw data in place, destroying the ability to start over. - Installing full Anaconda when Miniconda would do. ##### Hands-on Create a virtual environment inside a new project folder, activate it, install NumPy and Pandas, and generate a pinned `requirements.txt`. Then build a Jupyter notebook that documents a small analysis: a Markdown title and objective, one imports cell, a data-loading cell, three or four analysis cells each with Markdown explaining the reasoning, and a findings section. Finish by running Kernel → Restart and Run All and confirming it executes cleanly from top to bottom. For the mini-project, set up the full project structure above: `.gitignore`, `README.md` with setup instructions someone else could follow, pinned requirements, the `data/raw` and `data/processed` split, a numbered starter notebook, and a `src/helpers.py` with at least one function that the notebook imports. Initialise Git, install `nbstripout`, and make your first commit. Then delete your `.venv`, recreate it from `requirements.txt`, and verify the notebook still runs — that test is the whole point of everything above. For the assignment, write a short notebook that explains why virtual environments matter, using Markdown for the reasoning and code cells that actually demonstrate creating one, installing a package, and showing that it is isolated from the global installation. Teaching it is how you check that you understand it. ##### Key takeaways - One virtual environment per project, activated before every install, with pinned versions committed. - A Jupyter kernel holds state independently of your code — restart and run all before trusting any notebook. - Structure notebooks as documents: imports at the top, one idea per cell, Markdown explaining why. - Raw data is immutable; every transformation writes to a new location so you can always start again. - Colab is excellent for GPUs and sharing, but pin versions and remember the filesystem disappears.
